pr.title: Record how a passkey registration picks its entry
pr.head: ffebbc762f782faa7bec3cae0e28428acb6ca5ea

summary: The passkeys plan designs a small Mac and iPhone app whose AutoFill extension creates passkeys and signs in with them, keeping each one as a passkey field on an entry in the multipass store. The plan is a draft, waiting on a prototype.

When a site asks the extension to register a new passkey, the extension has to choose which entry the passkey goes into. The owner already decided that in the plan's open questions, § 6 questions 7 to 9, but the design sections an implementer reads, § 2 and § 4, never said it. This pull request writes those decisions into the design, without changing any of them.

• Which entry. The extension looks for an entry named after the site's relying party ID, the domain the passkey belongs to, such as github.com. With none, it creates one. With one that has no passkey, it adds the passkey there, beside the password and one-time password. With one that already holds a passkey, it uses an entry named <rp id> <user name>, such as github.com octocat-work.
  • One passkey per entry. Each entry holds at most one passkey field, so each entry still describes one account, and every entry holds at least one of secret, otp, and passkey.
  • Checks to match. Two acceptance rows and two store-reader tests cover joining an existing entry and a second account's entry.

The plan stays draft. The review left one open finding: the rule does not say what happens when the same account registers again, so the live passkey can land in a second entry and a third registration has no defined outcome.

cards.title: Terms on this page
cards.html:
• Relying party ID (rp ID): the domain a passkey belongs to, such as github.com. The system checks it against the page.
  • User handle: the opaque account ID the site sends when it registers a passkey, stored as the field's user part.
  • User name: the readable account name the site sends, such as octocat.
  • Entry: one named record in the store, holding a password, a one-time password, a passkey, or several of them.

cards.title: Related plans
cards.html:
• Websites (ready, not built) adds a website field in format 4 and moves the passkey field to format 5 when it ships. This plan still says format 4, which matches that order.
  • Mergeable store (completed) merges whole entries, newest wins, so two devices that register on the same site while one is offline keep only the newer passkey, as § 2.4 already says.
  • Session unlock (completed): the extension opens the store itself and never asks the session agent.

groups.title: The passkeys plan
groups.kicker: Step 5 of § 2.1, § 2.2, the § 2.5 file table, and § 4's rows and tests
intro: Every change is in the one plan file, and each restates a decision that § 6 already records. Read step 5 of § 2.1 first: it is the rule an implementer would follow. § 2.2 then gives the store's side of it, at most one passkey field per entry, and § 4 adds the checks that prove it.

files.note: The plan: the registration rule in § 2.1 step 5, the one-passkey rule in § 2.2, and matching rows in § 2.5 and § 4.

checks.text: § 2.1 step 5: the rule sends a registration to <rp id> <user name> whenever the entry already holds any passkey, without comparing that passkey's user handle with the new one. So registering the same account again puts the live passkey in a second entry and leaves the dead one beside the password, and a third registration finds <rp id> <user name> holding a passkey too, a case the plan does not define. The review asks the plan to say what happens in both cases, or to list them in § 6 with an owner.

§ 2.2: the entry name is the only key the rule uses. The websites plan adds website lines to entries, so an entry named github work that lists https://github.com would not get the passkey. The review lists reconciling the two as a follow-up.

§ 2.5: the src/store.rs row still names format 4, which matches the websites plan's § 2.4. That plan takes format 4 when it is built and moves this plan to format 5 then, and AGENTS.md still names format 3 as what multipass writes. Checked by reading both plans and AGENTS.md at the base.
